source_text: Propterea autem in superioribus voluntatem perfectam magis quam rerum effectus locavi, quoniam et parricidium et sacrilegium et adulterium vel horum similia facilius est cavere quam facere; neque enim semper voluntati malae perpetrandi quod vult adest facultas, at e regione horum abstinentia in summa quiete consistit, nisi forte hoc ipsum a vobis labor dicatur, laborare nolle. Omitto ea, quae tam Scripturae sanctae, quas Prophetae, quas Evangelistae, quas Apostoli protulerunt, quam disputatores catholica sanitate fulgentes, Ioannes, Basilius, Theodorus et horum similes, commendaverunt, multo esse maiorem laborem committere crimina quam cavere.
pass_a_gloss: On this account however in the superiors I placed a perfect will more than the effects of things, since both parricide and sacrilege and adultery or things similar to these it is easier to beware than to do; for not always is the faculty of perpetrating what it wants present to an evil will, but from the other side abstinence from these consists in highest quiet, unless perhaps this itself is said by you a labor, to be unwilling to labor. I omit those things which both the holy Scriptures, which the Prophets, which the Evangelists, which the Apostles have brought forth, and disputers shining with catholic health, John, Basil, Theodore and those similar to them, have commended, that it is a much greater labor to commit crimes than to beware.

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: In the preceding examples I emphasized a fully formed intention rather than the accomplishment of acts, because murder of a parent, sacrilege, adultery, and similar deeds are easier to avoid than to commit. An evil will does not always have the opportunity to carry out what it wants. Conversely, abstaining from these things involves complete quiet—unless you call the very unwillingness to toil a kind of toil. I pass over what holy Scripture, presented by prophets, evangelists, and apostles, and teachers shining with catholic soundness—John, Basil, Theodore, and others like them—have commended: committing crimes takes much greater effort than avoiding them.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's sacred writings; keep Scripture, not 'Bible' as a later book-name.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
